opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
God does not leave His people in the grave. He does not leave us sealed in darkness, enclosed in stone, buried in sin, grief, fear, or death. In Ezekiel He says, “O my people, I will open your graves and have you rise from them.” His people are not meant to remain in an enclosed cave. Our graves are meant to open. We are meant to rise.

This is why the Gospel of Lazarus is so piercing. Jesus does not rush. He waits. Mary and Martha wait. The mourners wait. In that waiting, there is anguish. Lazarus is not merely sick; he is four days dead. The situation has become impossible. And that is exactly where Jesus chooses to reveal Himself.

He waited not because He lacked love, but because He was revealing something greater than healing. He was showing that He is not merely one who helps the dying, but Lord over death itself. Had He gone at once, they would have seen healing. By waiting, they would see glory. They would learn that when God seems delayed, He is not absent.

Then there is Thomas: “Let us also go to die with him.” Thomas speaks with courage, yet without full understanding. His words carry more than he knows. To go with Christ is always to pass through death into life.

The psalm says, “More than sentinels wait for the dawn.” The sentinel stands in darkness, watching and waiting for the light he cannot force to come. That is Mary. That is Martha. That is every soul waiting on God through sorrow and grief. Their waiting was painful, but dawn was coming, and Christ was that dawn.

When Jesus arrives, the Jews see His tears and say, “See how much he loved him.” That is true, but they do not yet see who is weeping. They see sorrow, but not Glory standing before the tomb. Their blindness is that they measure Christ only by what He did not prevent, not by what He is about to reveal.

Jesus is deeply perturbed. He weeps, and He is troubled. He truly loved Lazarus. His tears are real. But His perturbance reaches deeper: He stands before the wreckage of sin and death and before hearts clouded by grief and blindness. Christ weeps, but not as one defeated. He weeps as one who has come to shatter the prison.

Then comes Romans: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh; you are in the Spirit, if only the Spirit of God dwells in you.” This means that man left to himself, bound in sin and apart from grace, cannot please God. Left there, we remain enclosed. But those who accept Christ receive not only His teaching, but His Spirit. And if His Spirit dwells in us, then His life is already at work in us.

So whether alive or dead, literally or figuratively, those who belong to Christ are not abandoned to the grave. Some are in tombs of sorrow, fear, sin, despair, or unbelief. Yet the word of the Lord remains: “I will open your graves and have you rise from them.” That is not poetry only. It is promise.

Jesus says it plainly: “I am the resurrection and the life.” He does not merely bring resurrection. He is Resurrection. He does not merely offer life. He is Life. Whoever believes in Him, even if he dies, will live.

The grave is not ultimate for His people. The stone does not get the final word. The tomb does not get the final word. The flesh does not get the final word. Christ does.

Not in an enclosed cave will we remain.
He will open our graves.
He will have us rise from them.
And those who belong to Christ will have everlasting life in Him.
